traditions.name: Karaite Judaism
traditions.note: The dispute with rabbinic Judaism is over the oral law and the Talmud, not over the written books, which is why it leaves no mark on this volume.
traditions.source: The dispute is over the Talmud and the oral Torah, not over the contents of the written canon.

traditions.name: Messianic Judaism
traditions.note: The Tanakh and the New Testament together, with the first part usually kept in the Jewish order and under its Hebrew names.
traditions.source: The canon is the Protestant one; the ordering and the names used for its divisions are not.

traditions.name: Samaritanism
traditions.note: Holds the Torah alone, in the Samaritan recension — a text that differs from the Masoretic Torah in some six thousand places. This volume prints the Masoretic text, so it cannot show you a Samaritan Bible, and pointing you at the Torah here would be showing you a different book under their name.
traditions.source: The Samaritan Pentateuch is a distinct textual recension, not a subset of the text printed here.

traditions.name: Presbyterian and Reformed churches
traditions.note: The Westminster Confession names the sixty-six and says the apocrypha are “of no authority in the Church of God” and not to be approved or made use of otherwise than other human writings — the firmest of the Protestant statements on the question.

traditions.name: Anglican and Episcopal churches
traditions.note: Anglican Bibles also print the apocrypha, which the Church “doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine” — read, and not doctrinal. That third category has no column here: this scope gives the sixty-six, and the Catholic one gives the books printed beside them.

traditions.name: Lutheran churches
traditions.note: Luther printed the apocrypha between the Testaments under a heading calling them “not held equal to the Scriptures, but useful and good to read” — the same third category the Anglican article names, and the reason Lutheran Bibles have varied in whether they print them at all.
traditions.source: Luther's German Bible (1534), the heading to the Apocrypha.

traditions.name: Eastern Catholic churches
traditions.note: In communion with Rome while keeping an Eastern liturgy — the difference from the Latin Church is of rite, not of which books.
traditions.source: The canon is that fixed at Trent, shared with the Latin Church.

traditions.name: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches
traditions.note: The widest canon there is, and the only one that receives 1 Enoch and Jubilees as scripture — which is much of why this volume prints them.
traditions.source: canon.json records the Ethiopian column; the coverage note on the Canons page states the enumeration.

traditions.name: The Coptic Orthodox Church
traditions.note: Oriental Orthodox rather than Eastern. The two canons are close and are not identical, and this volume does not draw the difference — so the scope below is an approximation, offered as one rather than as this church's own list.
traditions.source: This volume compares five canons; the Coptic canon is not one of its columns.

traditions.name: The Armenian Apostolic Church
traditions.note: Oriental Orthodox rather than Eastern, with a canon close to that column and not identical to it — so the scope below is an approximation. Some Armenian Bibles have also carried a third letter to the Corinthians, which this volume does not print.
traditions.source: This volume compares five canons; the Armenian canon is not one of its columns.

traditions.name: The Assyrian Church of the East
traditions.note: Reads the Peshitta, whose New Testament has twenty-two books: 2 Peter, 2 John, 3 John, Jude and Revelation are not in it. All five are printed in this volume, so none of the five columns can stand in for this canon — a scope built from any of them would hand you books this church does not receive.
traditions.source: The Peshitta New Testament omits the four shorter Catholic epistles and the Apocalypse.

traditions.name: Rastafari
traditions.note: Holds the Ethiopic Enoch and the Kebra Nagast in particular regard. This volume prints Enoch; it does not print the Kebra Nagast.
traditions.source: The scriptural canon is the Ethiopian Orthodox one.

traditions.name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
traditions.note: Holds the sixty-six as one part of a larger scripture that also includes the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price. Those three are nineteenth-century texts and are not in this volume, which stops in the second century.
traditions.source: The biblical canon is the Protestant sixty-six, in the King James translation.

traditions.name: Jehovah's Witnesses
traditions.note: Holds the same sixty-six books, in its own translation.
traditions.source: The canon is the Protestant sixty-six; the New World Translation is a translation, not a different canon.

traditions.name: Islam
traditions.note: Honours the Tawrat, Zabur and Injil given to Moses, David and Jesus, and holds that the texts in circulation are not those revelations intact. Its own scripture is the Qur'an, which is not in this volume: this is a library of Jewish and Christian scripture and does not pretend to be more.
traditions.source: The Qur'an is not among the texts this volume carries.
